In October 1950, a few months after the outbreak of the Korean War, French Prime Minister René Pleven proposed a European army in which West German soldiers would serve alongside those of other countries under a common command, rather than in a German national army. The aim was to meet American calls for a West German contribution to Western defence while avoiding the revival of an independent German military. Negotiations led to the treaty establishing the European Defence Community (EDC), signed in Paris in May 1952 by the six members of the European Coal and Steel Community.

The project went beyond military cooperation. A draft for a European Political Community, prepared in 1953, would have placed both the EDC and the coal and steel institutions within a common political framework. Yet support in France, the country that had launched the idea, weakened as the fighting in Korea ended and Stalin's death eased tensions. On 30 August 1954 the French National Assembly voted, without a full debate on the substance, to set the treaty aside, and the political community collapsed with it.

The question of German rearmament was settled within months by other means. Under agreements signed in Paris in October 1954, the Western European Union was set up, and West Germany joined NATO in May 1955 with armed forces of its own.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Support for the European army weakened in all six signatory states once East–West tensions began to ease.
Italy, like France, had not yet ratified the treaty when the French National Assembly voted in August 1954.
West Germany ended up with the kind of national armed forces that the Pleven plan had been designed to prevent.
The planned European Political Community survived the French vote and was later relaunched as the Western European Union.

After the failure of the defence community, the six coal and steel countries returned to economic cooperation. At a conference in Messina in June 1955, their foreign ministers asked a committee chaired by the Belgian Paul-Henri Spaak to examine the options, and its report became the basis for two treaties signed in Rome on 25 March 1957. One established the European Economic Community (EEC); the other created the European Atomic Energy Community, known as Euratom. Both entered into force on 1 January 1958.

The EEC Treaty was the more ambitious of the two. It provided for a common market in which goods, persons, services and capital could move freely, and for a customs union with a common external tariff, to be completed over a transitional period of twelve years. In the event, the last internal customs duties on industrial goods were abolished on 1 July 1968, ahead of schedule. Euratom, by contrast, was meant to pool research and develop civil nuclear energy, but national governments, France in particular, were reluctant to share control of a sector they regarded as strategic, and the community played a more modest role than its founders had hoped.

Unlike the coal and steel treaty, which was concluded for fifty years and expired in 2002, both Rome treaties were concluded for an unlimited period.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Internal customs duties on industrial goods in the EEC ended sooner than the treaty's timetable required.
National governments were reluctant to share control in every field covered by the two treaties signed in Rome.
The Spaak committee recommended setting up two separate communities rather than a single, broader one.
Euratom's founders expected nuclear power to meet most of Europe's energy needs within a few decades.

By the early 1960s three European Communities existed side by side: the European Coal and Steel Community, set up in 1952, and the European Economic Community and Euratom, both operating since 1958. They already shared two institutions. Under a convention signed together with the Rome treaties, a single parliamentary assembly and a single Court of Justice served all three. Each Community, however, still had its own executive and its own council of ministers: the coal and steel community was run by a High Authority, while the two newer Communities each had a Commission.

The treaty signed in Brussels on 8 April 1965, usually called the Merger Treaty, replaced the three executives with a single Commission and the three councils with a single Council. It entered into force on 1 July 1967, and the Belgian Jean Rey became the first President of the merged Commission. The treaty also gave a formal basis to the committee of national permanent representatives that prepares the Council's work.

The merger concerned the institutions, not the Communities themselves. The three remained distinct legal entities, each governed by its own founding treaty, so the single Commission applied different rules depending on which treaty it was acting under. The coal and steel community came to an end when its treaty expired in 2002, while Euratom still exists today alongside the European Union.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: By the early 1960s, the three Communities already shared most of their institutions with one another.
The Merger Treaty created the common Court of Justice of the three European Communities.
Euratom is now the only one of the three original Communities that remains a separate legal entity.
Before July 1967, the coal and steel community and Euratom never shared the same executive body.

The Treaty on European Union, signed in Maastricht in February 1992, created the European Union and gave it an unusual structure, often described as a temple resting on three pillars. The first pillar consisted of the existing Communities, with the European Economic Community renamed the European Community to reflect its wider scope. Here the established 'Community method' applied: the Commission had the right of initiative, the Council frequently decided by qualified majority, and the Court of Justice could enforce the rules.

The two new pillars worked differently. The second covered a common foreign and security policy, and the third covered cooperation in justice and home affairs, including asylum, immigration, and police and judicial cooperation. In both, decision-making was essentially intergovernmental: the Council generally acted by unanimity, the Commission either shared the right of initiative with Member States or had none, and the Parliament and the Court played only a limited role. Governments wanted to work together in these sensitive areas without handing them over to supranational institutions.

Ratification was not smooth. Danish voters rejected the treaty in June 1992 and approved it in a second referendum in May 1993, after Denmark had obtained several opt-outs, and the treaty entered into force on 1 November 1993. Later revisions moved parts of the third pillar into the Community framework, before the pillar structure was abolished altogether in 2009.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The French referendum held in September 1992 approved the Maastricht Treaty by a very narrow margin.
When the Union was created, asylum fell under procedures that gave the Court of Justice little say.
The United Kingdom was probably the main advocate of making the two new pillars intergovernmental.
In the second and third pillars, the Commission was always excluded from proposing measures.

The Treaty of Amsterdam, signed in 1997, extended the powers of the European Parliament and moved asylum and immigration into the Community framework, but it left unresolved the institutional reforms needed for a much larger Union. These 'Amsterdam leftovers', chiefly the size of the Commission, the weighting of votes in the Council and the extension of qualified majority voting, were the main business of the intergovernmental conference that ended in Nice in December 2000.

The resulting treaty, signed in February 2001, reweighted Council votes in favour of the larger Member States and extended qualified majority voting to a number of further provisions, while unanimity remained the rule in sensitive areas such as taxation. It also provided for a Commission with one member per Member State, so the five largest countries would give up their second Commissioner. Many observers found the outcome complicated and modest, and the summit was remembered for difficult late-night bargaining.

Ireland was the only Member State to put the treaty to a referendum. In June 2001 Irish voters rejected it on a turnout of about one third. After the government obtained declarations confirming that the treaty did not affect Ireland's traditional policy of military neutrality, a second referendum in October 2002 approved it by a clear majority, and the treaty entered into force on 1 February 2003.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Nice Treaty moved all remaining areas of Council decision-making to qualified majority voting.
Most of the Irish electorate voted against the Nice Treaty in the first referendum, held in June 2001.
The Charter of Fundamental Rights was solemnly proclaimed at the same European summit in Nice.
The size of the Commission was already an open question before the negotiations that ended in Nice.

On 1 May 2004 ten countries joined the European Union: Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia. It remains the largest single enlargement in the Union's history, raising the number of Member States from 15 to 25 and adding around 75 million people, although the newcomers' combined economic output was small compared with that of the existing members.

The accession treaty allowed the existing Member States to restrict, for a transitional period of up to seven years, access to their labour markets for workers from eight of the new members; the restrictions did not apply to Cyprus and Malta. Most of the existing Member States used this option at first, though many lifted their restrictions before the period ended. The United Kingdom, Ireland and Sweden opened their labour markets immediately, and the United Kingdom received far more workers than an official forecast had predicted.

Cyprus joined as a divided island. A United Nations plan to reunify it was put to separate referendums in the two communities a week before accession: Turkish Cypriots approved it, but Greek Cypriots rejected it by a large majority. The whole island joined the EU, but the application of EU law is suspended in the northern areas, which are not under the effective control of the government of the Republic of Cyprus.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Bulgaria and Romania, whose preparations took longer, joined the Union three years after the other ten.
Of the ten 2004 entrants, only Cyprus and Malta were exempt from the transitional rules on workers.
Workers from the new members were kept out of most old Member States' labour markets for seven years.
Greek Cypriots rejected the reunification plan, whereas Turkish Cypriots backed it unanimously.

The Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe was signed in Rome in October 2004. It was intended to replace the existing treaties with a single text, to give the Union a single legal personality and to make the Charter of Fundamental Rights legally binding. Like other treaties amending the founding treaties, it had to be ratified by every Member State, either by a parliamentary vote or, where national rules or political choices required it, by a referendum.

The early results were encouraging for its supporters. Spanish voters approved it in February 2005 by a large majority, although fewer than half of those entitled to vote took part. Then, within a week, the treaty was rejected in France on 29 May 2005 by about 55% of voters and in the Netherlands on 1 June by about 62%, on turnouts considerably higher than in Spain. Analyses of the French vote suggested that many voters were motivated by domestic concerns such as unemployment, as well as by objections to the text itself.

Luxembourg nevertheless approved the treaty in a referendum in July 2005, but several governments postponed their planned votes, and the European Council called for a 'period of reflection'. The constitutional project was eventually abandoned, although much of its institutional content was later carried over into a conventional amending treaty.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Luxembourg's voters approved the treaty after voters in two other countries had rejected it.
The Dutch vote on the treaty was the first national referendum held in the Netherlands in modern times.
Supporters of the treaty may have lost the French vote mainly because of a poorly organised campaign.
The French rejection of the treaty was caused entirely by domestic concerns such as unemployment.

The European Chips Act entered into force in September 2023. Its headline aim is to double the EU's share of global semiconductor production capacity, from around 10% to 20% by 2030, in a market that is itself expected to grow strongly. The Act has three strands. The first, the Chips for Europe Initiative, supports research, pilot lines and design capacity, bridging the gap between laboratory and factory. The second sets a framework for 'first-of-a-kind' production facilities, which can benefit from faster permitting and, within EU state aid rules, from public support granted by Member States. The third creates a mechanism to monitor supply chains and respond to shortages, coordinated by a European Semiconductor Board.

The Commission has said the Act should mobilise more than €43 billion of public and private investment. Most of that sum, however, is expected to come from Member States and industry rather than from the EU budget.

Critics argue that the target is unrealistic. In a report published in 2025, the European Court of Auditors concluded that the 20% goal was unlikely to be reached, and some large factory projects announced in recent years have since been delayed or cancelled. Supporters reply that the Act was also meant to strengthen resilience and monitoring, not merely to reach a single market-share figure.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Act was drawn up in response to chip shortages that halted car production during the pandemic.
The first strand of the Act mainly finances the construction of large-scale chip production plants.
Most of the investment that the Act is meant to mobilise will not be paid for by the EU budget.
The Court of Auditors concluded in 2025 that the Chips Act had failed in all of its objectives.

The NIS2 Directive, which replaced the EU's first directive on network and information security, had to be transposed into national law by October 2024. Many Member States missed that deadline, and the Commission opened infringement procedures against most of them. The directive widens the range of sectors covered, from energy, transport, banking and health to waste management, food production, space and parts of the digital economy, and divides the organisations concerned into 'essential' and 'important' entities.

As a rule, NIS2 applies to medium-sized and large organisations in the listed sectors, and small companies fall outside it. There are exceptions, however: some providers, such as top-level domain name registries and providers of public electronic communications networks, are covered whatever their size. Covered entities must take appropriate measures to manage cybersecurity risks, and their management bodies must approve those measures and can be held responsible for failures to comply.

Reporting is staged. A significant incident must be notified to the competent authority or to the national computer security incident response team: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, a fuller notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month. Member States must provide for maximum fines of at least €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for essential entities, and €7 million or 1.4% for important entities.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The early warning must state whether the incident may have been a criminal act.
A top-level domain registry with twenty employees still has to comply with the directive.
Under NIS2, every organisation in the listed sectors must take cybersecurity risk-management measures.
Management bodies can be held responsible for any cyber incident that affects their organisation.

The Cyber Resilience Act, which entered into force in December 2024, sets cybersecurity requirements for 'products with digital elements': hardware and software that can connect, directly or indirectly, to another device or to a network. It covers items as varied as smart toys, home routers, operating systems and password managers. Products already regulated by sector-specific rules with comparable requirements, such as medical devices and motor vehicles, are excluded, and so is free and open-source software that is not supplied in the course of a commercial activity.

The Act applies in stages. Manufacturers' duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, both to a designated national computer security incident response team and to ENISA, the EU cybersecurity agency, applies from September 2026, whereas most other obligations apply from December 2027. Manufacturers must design products to be secure and handle vulnerabilities throughout a support period that reflects how long the product is expected to be in use, normally at least five years, providing security updates during that time.

For most products, manufacturers may assess their own compliance before affixing the CE marking. Certain categories listed as 'important' or 'critical', such as firewalls, face stricter procedures, which may require an assessment by an independent body.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Under the Act, all software sold in the EU must receive security updates for at least five years.
Open-source software is excluded from the Act even when it is supplied as part of a commercial activity.
Manufacturers that fail to provide security updates can be fined up to €15 million.
A maker of connected toys will have reporting duties before most of its other obligations apply.

Under the revised EU regulation on electronic identification, which entered into force in May 2024, every Member State must offer its citizens and residents at least one European Digital Identity Wallet by the end of 2026. The wallet is an application, typically on a smartphone, that lets users identify themselves online and in person, store digital documents such as a driving licence or a university diploma, and sign documents electronically.

The wallet must be free of charge for individuals, and its use is voluntary: people who choose not to use it must not be disadvantaged when they access public or private services. A central design principle is selective disclosure. A user should be able to prove a single attribute, for instance that they are over 18, without revealing other data such as their full date of birth or their address. Wallet providers may not collect information about how the wallet is used beyond what is needed to provide the service.

Acceptance is being phased in. Public services that require electronic identification must accept the wallet, and so, when users ask to use it, must very large online platforms and private services that are legally required to authenticate users strongly, such as banks. Member States are building their wallets on common technical specifications, so that a wallet issued in one country can be used across the Union.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The new digital wallets will eventually replace the national identity cards issued by Member States.
The wallet can also be used to make payments, both in shops and online, across the Union.
Individuals never have to pay to obtain and use a European Digital Identity Wallet.
All private online services operating in the EU will be obliged to accept the wallet.

The Data Act, which has applied since September 2025, sets rules on who may access and use the data generated by connected products, such as cars, smart household appliances and industrial machinery, and by related services. Users of such products, whether consumers or businesses, are entitled to access the data their use generates and may ask for it to be shared with a third party of their choice, for example an independent repair service. Connected products placed on the market after September 2026 must be designed so that, where technically feasible, this data is directly accessible to users by default.

The right has limits. Trade secrets remain protected, and a data holder may refuse to share them where disclosure would very probably cause it serious economic damage, provided it can justify that decision. Companies designated as gatekeepers under the EU's digital competition rules are not eligible to receive data as third parties under this right.

The Act also aims to make it easier to switch between cloud providers. Providers must remove obstacles to switching, and charges for switching are being phased out: until January 2027 they may not exceed the costs directly linked to the switch, and from then on they are not allowed at all. Finally, public bodies may request data from companies in situations of exceptional need, such as a public emergency.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A car owner could not use the Act's sharing right to have vehicle data passed to a designated gatekeeper.
The Data Act is mainly intended to help small firms compete with the largest technology companies.
All connected products sold in the EU must now be designed so that users can access their data by default.
Public bodies may require companies to hand over data whenever they consider it useful for their work.

The European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, known as EuroHPC, was set up in 2018 and is based in Luxembourg. It pools resources from the EU, participating countries and private partners to acquire and operate world-class supercomputers, which are hosted by national computing centres across Europe. Its systems include LUMI in Kajaani, Finland, Leonardo in Bologna, Italy, and MareNostrum 5 in Barcelona, Spain. JUPITER, installed at Jülich in Germany, was designed as Europe's first exascale machine, able to perform a billion billion calculations per second, and a second exascale system is planned in France.

Computing time on these machines is allocated mainly through calls for proposals assessed on scientific merit, and access for research is generally free of charge for users based in the EU and in participating countries. Scientists use the machines for climate modelling, drug discovery, materials science and other demanding tasks.

In 2024 the joint undertaking's mandate was extended to artificial intelligence. It now supports 'AI Factories', which give start-ups, researchers and industry access to computing resources suited to training large AI models, and it has also begun to acquire quantum computers to be integrated with its supercomputers. Energy use is a recurring concern: LUMI, for example, runs on hydroelectric power, and the waste heat it produces helps to warm homes in the surrounding area.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: EuroHPC's supercomputers run on hydroelectric power and use their waste heat to warm nearby homes.
JUPITER, installed at Jülich, is at present the fastest supercomputer in operation anywhere in the world.
Most of the joint undertaking's funding probably comes from the EU budget rather than from member countries.
A Spain-based climate scientist could apply for research time on a machine in Finland free of charge.

In the early twentieth century, Henrietta Swan Leavitt, working at the Harvard College Observatory, studied large numbers of variable stars on photographic plates of the Small Magellanic Cloud. Among them was a class now called Cepheid variables, which brighten and dim in a regular cycle. In 1912 she reported that the brighter Cepheids had longer periods. Because the stars in the Cloud are all at roughly the same distance from Earth, differences in their apparent brightness had to reflect real differences in the light they emit.

This period–luminosity relation made Cepheids usable as 'standard candles'. By timing a Cepheid's cycle, astronomers could infer how much light it actually gives off; comparing that with how bright it appears then reveals its distance. At first, however, Leavitt's relation gave only relative distances, and it had to be calibrated using nearby Cepheids whose distances could be measured independently.

In the 1920s Edwin Hubble identified Cepheids in what was then called the Andromeda Nebula and showed that it lay far beyond the Milky Way, settling a long debate about whether such spiral nebulae were separate galaxies. Later work revealed that there are two types of Cepheids, each with its own relation, and correcting the earlier confusion between them roughly doubled the estimated distances to other galaxies in the 1950s.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: On its own, Leavitt's 1912 finding did not tell astronomers how far away a particular Cepheid was.
Distance estimates based on Cepheids have remained essentially unchanged since Hubble's work in the 1920s.
Leavitt's contribution was largely overlooked by other astronomers during her lifetime.
Cepheid variables allow astronomers to measure the distance to any galaxy in the universe.

The first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star was announced in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, who later shared a Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. Planets had been detected three years earlier around a pulsar, the collapsed remnant of a massive star, but 51 Pegasi b was the first found around an ordinary star like the Sun. It was detected with the radial velocity method: as a planet orbits, it tugs its star slightly back and forth, and the wavelength of the star's light shifts accordingly. This method gives a lower limit for the planet's mass.

Most of the more than 6,000 exoplanets confirmed since then have been found with the transit method, which watches for the slight, regular dimming that occurs when a planet passes in front of its star. A transit reveals the planet's size relative to the star, but it can be seen only if the orbit is aligned almost edge-on from our point of view, so many planetary systems can never be detected in this way.

Both methods find large planets on close orbits more easily than small, distant ones, because these produce stronger and more frequent signals. When a planet is detected by both methods, astronomers can combine its mass and size to estimate its density, and hence whether it is more likely to be rocky or gaseous.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The transit method was first used successfully by the Kepler space telescope to find new planets.
Mayor and Queloz made their 1995 discovery using a telescope placed in orbit around the Earth.
The planets known today are likely to under-represent small planets that orbit far from their stars.
A planet can be detected by the transit method only if its orbit is exactly edge-on as seen from Earth.

Radiocarbon dating, developed by the American chemist Willard Libby in the late 1940s, earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960. It relies on carbon-14, a radioactive form of carbon produced in the upper atmosphere through the action of cosmic rays on nitrogen. Plants absorb carbon-14 along with ordinary carbon through photosynthesis, and animals take it in by eating plants, so living organisms keep roughly the same proportion of carbon-14 as their surroundings. When an organism dies it stops taking in carbon, and the carbon-14 it contains decays at a known rate, halving about every 5,730 years. Measuring how much remains therefore indicates how long ago death occurred.

The method can be applied only to material that once contained carbon from living things, such as wood, bone, charcoal or textiles. After about 50,000 years so little carbon-14 is left that it can no longer be measured reliably. Moreover, the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has varied over time, so raw results must be calibrated against records of known age, such as tree rings.

Modern accelerator mass spectrometry counts carbon-14 atoms directly and needs only milligrams of material, compared with the grams required by earlier techniques. This has made it possible to date precious objects while causing only minimal damage.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Nuclear weapons tests in the mid-twentieth century sharply raised atmospheric carbon-14 levels.
Charcoal from a hearth about 70,000 years old would be beyond the method's reliable range.
Uncalibrated radiocarbon results are always wrong by several centuries, whatever the sample.
Accelerator mass spectrometry allows precious objects to be dated without damaging them.

Anchoring is the tendency for an initial number to pull later estimates towards it, even when that number is plainly irrelevant. In a well-known experiment reported in 1974, the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune, rigged to stop at either 10 or 65, in front of participants. They then asked them whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than the number on the wheel, and finally to estimate the actual percentage. Participants who had seen 10 gave a median estimate of 25%; those who had seen 65 gave a median estimate of 45%.

Later studies have found anchoring effects among experienced professionals as well as students. In one study, estate agents' valuations of a house were influenced by the asking price they were shown, although most of them said the price had played no part in their judgement. Anchors appear to work partly by making information consistent with the anchor easier to call to mind.

Simply warning people about the bias does little to reduce it. A strategy that has shown some success is to 'consider the opposite', deliberately listing reasons why the anchor might be inappropriate, although this weakens the effect rather than eliminating it.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every participant who saw 65 gave a higher estimate than every participant who had seen 10.
Kahneman's research on judgement later earned him a Nobel Prize in economic sciences.
Participants who were paid for accurate answers were less influenced by the number on the wheel.
Not all of the estate agents acknowledged that the asking price had influenced them.

Regression to the mean is a statistical phenomenon first described by Francis Galton in the 1880s. Studying the heights of parents and their adult children, he found that very tall parents tended to have children who were tall, but on average less extreme than themselves, while very short parents tended to have children who were short but closer to the average. Galton initially read this as a biological tendency towards mediocrity, but the effect is statistical. It arises whenever two measurements are imperfectly correlated, because an extreme result usually owes something to chance factors that are unlikely to recur.

The phenomenon often misleads people who evaluate interventions. Daniel Kahneman described flight instructors who believed that praise harmed performance and criticism improved it, since a trainee praised after an excellent landing usually did worse the next time, while one criticised after a poor landing usually did better. Both patterns would be expected even if feedback had no effect at all.

The same trap arises in public policy. Road junctions are often selected for speed cameras after an unusually bad year for accidents. A fall in accidents the following year is then partly to be expected anyway, so a credible evaluation must compare the treated junctions with similar sites that received no camera, or use data covering a longer period.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Galton's first explanation of the pattern he found in parents' and children's heights was a statistical one.
A school chosen for extra help after one very bad year would be expected to improve even if the help did nothing.
The flight instructors' praise and criticism in fact had no effect on how well their trainees landed afterwards.
Regression to the mean means that an extreme result is always followed by a result close to the average.

Most of a human cell's DNA is packed into the nucleus, but mitochondria, the structures that supply cells with energy, carry a small genome of their own. In humans it is a circular molecule of roughly 16,600 base pairs containing 37 genes, compared with about three billion base pairs in the nuclear genome. A cell may contain hundreds or thousands of copies of mitochondrial DNA but only two copies of the nuclear genome.

Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost exclusively from the mother, because the father's mitochondria are normally eliminated after fertilisation; only a handful of cases of paternal transmission have been reported. It therefore passes down the female line largely unchanged, apart from occasional mutations, and is not reshuffled in each generation as nuclear DNA is.

These properties make it valuable to forensic scientists and archaeologists. Because there are so many copies, it can often be recovered from old or degraded samples when nuclear DNA cannot. A skeleton found under a car park in Leicester in 2012 was later identified as that of King Richard III, in part by comparing its mitochondrial DNA with that of living descendants of his eldest sister through an unbroken female line. Mitochondrial DNA cannot, however, distinguish between people who share the same maternal ancestry, such as siblings.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Mitochondrial DNA passes from mother to child entirely unchanged, in every family and every generation.
The identification of Richard III's skeleton also relied on radiocarbon dating of the bones.
Mitochondrial DNA alone could not show whether the skeleton was Richard III's or a full brother's.
Mitochondrial DNA can be recovered from old or degraded samples whenever nuclear DNA cannot be.

In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once formed a single landmass and had since drifted apart. He set out his case in a book first published in 1915. His evidence was varied: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle; similar fossils of land animals and plants occur on continents now separated by oceans; rock formations match across the Atlantic; and traces of ancient glaciers appear in regions that are now tropical.

Most geologists rejected the idea for decades. Their main objection was not to the evidence of past connections, which some explained by land bridges that had since sunk, but to the lack of a plausible mechanism: Wegener could not explain convincingly what force could move continents through the solid ocean floor, and the forces he suggested were shown to be far too weak. Wegener died on an expedition to Greenland in 1930, with his theory still widely dismissed.

The picture changed in the 1950s and 1960s, when surveys of the ocean floor revealed mid-ocean ridges and symmetrical bands of magnetised rock on either side of them. These findings showed that new crust forms at the ridges and spreads outwards, which supplied the kind of mechanism that had been missing. By the end of the 1960s, plate tectonics, which incorporated continental drift, had become the accepted framework of geology.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Wegener never saw continental drift accepted as part of mainstream geology.
Wegener's book was widely translated and was read by many geologists outside Germany.
Wegener's theory was rejected by all geologists from its publication until the 1950s.
Most geologists explained the matching fossils by land bridges that had since sunk.

In 1966 the psychologist Peter Wason devised a simple-looking test of logical reasoning. Participants see four cards, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other, showing for example E, K, 4 and 7. They are told a rule: 'If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side.' Their task is to turn over those cards, and no others, that are needed to find out whether the rule has been broken.

The correct answer is E and 7. The E card must be checked because an odd number on its back would break the rule, and so must the 7, because a vowel on its back would also break it. The 4 is irrelevant: the rule says nothing about what must lie behind an even number. In many studies, fewer than one participant in ten has chosen correctly; the most common answers are E alone, or E and 4.

Performance changes dramatically when the same logical structure is presented as a familiar social rule. If participants imagine checking that 'anyone drinking beer must be over 18', most correctly decide to check the beer drinker and the person under 18, not the cola drinker or the adult. Researchers still disagree about why. Some argue that people have a specialised ability to detect cheaters; others stress familiarity with rules about permission and obligation.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: In every study of the abstract version, fewer than one participant in ten has managed to choose correctly.
Researchers now agree that people do better on the drinking version because they are good at spotting cheaters.
Students who have been trained in formal logic solve the abstract version much more often than others do.
A participant who turned over E, 4 and 7 would have turned over one more card than the task required.
